items.quote: Now you may be wondering why I gave Elden Ring a 0/10 rating. When I first put the game in, I was genuinely amazed. I thought it was awesome. Extraordinary, even. I was like “yeah, this is it, this is peak gaming.” The world looked insane, the combat felt intense, everything was mysterious and cool and I was fully locked in from the start. But then I ran into one small problem that completely ruined my entire experience. I thought there was going to be a powerful, legendary, wearable ring called the Elden Ring. Like an actual ring. Something you equip. Something that gives you insane stats. Something that makes you basically unstoppable and cool-looking at the same time. That’s what I signed up for. So naturally, I started looking for it. At first it was casual. Just exploring. Doing a few fights. Checking the map. “I’ll find it soon,” I thought. But then it escalated. I started clearing entire regions. Killing bosses. Reading item descriptions I didn’t understand. Talking to NPCs like they were going to drop hints. It became personal. And the worst part is—I think I was too far gone to stop. I should’ve paid more attention to the story and the cutscenes, but instead I got locked into this idea that the Elden Ring was somewhere out there, just waiting to be found and equipped. So I kept pushing forward, thinking “it has to be next area, it has to be this boss, it has to be this dungeon.”Hours turned into days. Days turned into way too many hours. And then I finally reached the end of the game. And what do I find? Not a ring. Not even close. Just some giant dumbass yellow tree situation called the Elden Ring or something. At that point I was already in too deep. 300+ hours gone. Fully invested. Emotionally committed. And the “Elden Ring” turns out to be a metaphysical concept tied to a ugly ass yellow tree that you absolutely cannot wear on your finger. And even if it wasn’t broken or whatever… I still can’t wear it. Which feels like a major design oversight, if you ask me. So yeah. That’s why I give this game a 0/10.

items.quote: I know that this may make me sound like a loser, but it is true that the game "Elden Ring" changed my life. I first played elden ring when it had just released, and I made my character, did the tutorial, died to the tree sentinel, and didn't bother to pick it up again for two years. When I did finally try it again, I would say it was the greatest decision of my life. If it was not for elden ring, I would probably be playing assassin's creed or something right now. The strengths of Elden Ring are great enough in amount, that few weaknesses show, even after my almost 500 hours of playtime. So, to start this review off, the strengths: Elden Ring is a beautiful game. When you first start the game, you are in limgrave, an area that, though generic and bland compared to other areas, still is a nice way to start the game. You are naturally enticed by the site of the erdtree, and go that direction, leading you towards the first real boss most players will face, margit. Once you beat margit, you can go through the castle, and fight godrick, a remembrance boss. After you kill him, you can walk through the back of the castle, and find yourself in the next area: liurnia. This area is, simply put, beautiful. From there, you kill renalla, reach altis plateau, go into the capital, and kill the bosses there, leading you to the mountaintop of the giants. Once you kill fire giant, you are sent to the crumbling farum azula, and fight the bosses there, to return to the capital, and beat the game. This is the quickest route to beat the game, yet it is far from the only one. Immediately from when you start, you can go south, to the weeping peninsula, go east to called and dragonbarrow, or skip straight to liurnia. Or, you could go to the siofra river, through an elevator in a forest. This is another strength to elden ring: you are able to do just about anything, just about whenever. You could kill radahn and rykard before you even see margit. In the mountaintops, you can find a fort with the boss commander niall, killing him will give you half of a medallion. When you find the other half, you can go to one of the grand lifts, and access a secret area. Another strength is the density of some areas exploration. I was able to explore the capital for two and a half hours before being confident id found everything it had to offer. There is no shortage of amazing bosses in this game either. Hourah loux is one of the greatest bosses in the game, and one of the best bosses across fromsoft titles. Where games like bloodborne and dark souls have a bit of a quality drop in their second half, elden ring is different. I'd say the best way to split elden ring is thirds. The early game has some decent bosses, and some bad bosses, not very many great ones. I would consider the early game to be limgrave, caelid, and liurnia. Once you enter altus plateau, it is the mid-game. The capital has some of the best bosses, and the optional areas are incredibly cool. Though, many of these bosses aren't of the highest quality. Once you kill the fire giant, all the bosses feel like they are much better than before, with the sole exception of the godskin duo. Maliketh, the black blade, and hourah loux, warrior are some of the greatest bosses to ever be made. The combat, seemingly simple at first, is actually quite complex. There are talismans, weapon types, damage types, affinities, and status effects, that certain enemies might be weak to, or resistant to, or in some cases, entirely safe from. The physics flask allows you to find other items to buff you. Along with this there are actual items that buff you, too. Now, the weaknesses. I'd say the most glaring issue is that the sheer quantity of bosses means that some, of course, are pretty horrible, and often times are even recycled. Sometimes, the hit boxes are incredibly strange, and often times don't make sense. Some areas are convoluted, and some are very empty. Even with these issues, there are so many strengths to this game, I believe that all of these can be entirely overlooked. Elden Ring is possibly the greatest game ever created, and I will be dead before I say otherwise.

items.quote:
-no believable world, repetitive gameplay-
As a side note: my criticism isn't about difficulty. The game is fairly easy after the early game. I was already level 55 with under 15 hours, 83 by 20h (besides exploration - farming soldiers in Gatefront Ruins and militia in Greyoll's Dragonbarrow for fast runes).
The game has positive aspects, but for me the weaknesses clearly outweigh them.
The most positive point first: the monster design is magnificent. Many creatures, bosses, and enemies look fantastic and have an impressive presence. I also like the system with the spirit companions. That is already where the strengths end.

The world does not feel alive, but artificially pieced together. Instead of a believable fantasy world, I see a collection of enemies, ruins, and loot subjects/objects without meaning or connection. It feels as if everything is only there for grinding. There is hardly any normal life, hardly any society, hardly anything that gives the impression that this world is not just a backdrop for battles. The NPCs are often blurry and also seem placed into the landscape arbitrarily. Right at the beginning, you encounter a merchant who looks like Santa Claus.
What is especially disturbing for me is the artificial enemy AI. In some cases, the enemies behave absurdly stupidly. They stand in immediate proximity while you slaughter their comrades. These die screaming loudly, fall to the ground dramatically, and even break entire wooden carts into pieces in the process – yet the other enemies seem to take no notice of it at all. Once an enemy has spotted the player, it is often enough to crouch briefly – no matter whether you are crouching directly in their field of vision! (as long as you maintain a certain distance). Even if you are actually still in direct line of sight, they suddenly lose all interest, turn around, and walk away. If they randomly walk in the same direction as the player, it is usually enough to make a small detour around them, and you can already assassinate them from behind.

The progression system also did not convince me. Neither leveling attributes nor upgrading weapons feels particularly noticeable in combat. At the same time, the combat strength of many enemies often seems arbitrary. Instead of a comprehensible increase in power, the impression of an unbalanced system often arises.

For this very reason, I do not experience Elden Ring as challenging in the sense of a fair, high difficulty level. Instead, much of it feels unbalanced, inconsistent, and unnecessarily unfriendly to the player. Not to mention the imprecise controls. The game often does not challenge the player through intelligent systems or believable challenges, but rather through idiosyncratic design decisions that create frustration without increasing enjoyment accordingly.

On top of that comes the storytelling approach. After many hours, I never had the feeling of following an exciting story. Instead, you run around, collect items, upgrade weapons, level up, and defeat monsters. But for what purpose, actually? The story here is a pale excuse to at least have a bad explanation of what you are supposed to do in this world. The whole game principle ultimately boils down to finding stronger equipment in order to defeat stronger enemies, so that you can find even stronger equipment in order to defeat even stronger enemies. I found this cycle pointless and not very motivating.

However, if you are as ambitious as I am, you run the risk of spending hours upon hours farming runes or searching for useful items, not because it is fun, but because you simply want to progress.

The rune system sounds interesting on paper: when you die, the runes remain at the place of death. In practice, this mostly just means additional running distances.

It gets even more absurd in dungeons. If you jump down a small ledge, there is often no way back. The character can fight gigantic monsters, but cannot climb a chest-high rock. Such limitations do not feel challenging to me, but simply unnatural and unuser-friendly. It is better to always enter a dungeon without runes, because if you are still too weak for the enemies inside (which you cannot know, since in the same regions absurdly weak and absurdly strong enemies coexist), then you might lose all your runes.

Graphically, I am also conflicted. The landscapes and monsters can look impressive, but many NPCs and some enemies (knights, wolves) feel stiff, strange, and in some cases noticeably weaker in quality than the creatures. This creates a strange contrast for me between excellent monster design and less convincing character models.

Conclusion:
Hardly any atmospheric sense of travel, no believable world, repetitive gameplay loop. Technically and artistically impressive in individual areas, but as a gameplay experience for me neither motivating nor satisfying. The beautiful monsters alone are not enough to compensate for the many weaknesses.

items.quote: I played this title on my PS5.I think it's worth mentioning beforehand that I've already completed several Souls-like games, so the core gameplay mechanics weren't intimidating to me. Because of that, I wouldn't describe the game as particularly difficult. Funny enough, I actually found it easier than many other titles in the genre.Plot:It's **** with most Souls games, the story is difficult to rate because, in many ways, it barely exists. You wake up in a hostile world and need to destroy anything standing in your way. That's essentially the plot. Everything else is world-building and **** Elden Ring, they clearly tried to do something more ambitious, especially with George R. R. Martin's involvement. Unfortunately, for me, it didn't really land. In a game of this scale, it's a shame that so much of the story is hidden away in a few lines of item descriptions. They could have done much more with it.Graphics:They were good enough. Not outstanding, but not disappointing either. I've seen both better and worse.Optimization:This is where things become messy. The supposed 30 FPS cap felt more like a suggestion than an actual limit, as I experienced several noticeable frame-rate drops throughout my playthrough. While it wasn't completely game-breaking, it was definitely noticeable and occasionally distracting.Artistic Style:Now this is where the game truly shines. I absolutely loved the visual design. The enemy designs, environments, and overall atmosphere were excellent. Even when certain assets, such as ruins and environmental pieces, started to feel somewhat repetitive, it was never noticeable enough to hurt the experience.Gameplay:I'm always surprised by how enjoyable gameplay can be when developers focus on doing a few things really well instead of trying to do everything. Despite the relatively limited moveset, the combat remained engaging throughout the game. There are certainly some weaker moments, but above all else, it was simply fun. And sometimes that's more important than complexity.Overall:Even though there were signs that the game might have been a bit too ambitious for the size of the development team, I think they delivered. It's not the greatest game ever made, and personally I don't think it deserved all of the Game of the Year praise it received. However, I still enjoyed it a lot and would happily recommend it to fans of the genre.

items.quote:
Insane art direction, incredible sound design and phenomenal atmosphere. 

However, I hate how bosses and most enemies have crazy combos that never end and never give you a second to hit back. Also, I don't think a simple encounter in the wilds should feel as difficult as an endgame boss from earlier Souls games.

I don't like the open-world structure. Most of your time is spent riding your horse and wasting time trying to find something to do that doesn't involve just killing everything you see.

Quests are impossible to follow or complete without using the wiki. If you don't, you will either completely miss the next objective or randomly stumble on the NPC like 50 hours later and now they're dead.

Another thing. In previous Souls games, items and gear were found naturally through exploring all nooks and crannies. There doesn't seem to be as much stuff in the environment to find this time around, I'm never rewarded for going out of my way to explore, unless you count rewards from completing dungeons... which, most of the time, end up useless to you because of stats requirements. This creates a frustrating gameplay loop where you work your butt off to clear a difficult boss only to get a reward you won't even use. This happens over and over again unless you use a wiki to plan out your build and route but that defeats the whole point of exploration.

Finally, I think the game takes too long to beat. I prefer the previous Souls games that are more focused and intentional. Elden Ring feels bloated.

items.quote: I have a love hate relationship with Elden Ring. It has some of the coolest weapons/builds in all Fromsoft history and NG+7 is actually doable and fun to play through, but that's where the positives end. Open world games are overwhelming nowadays for someone who likes to complete games. Waaaay too many copy pasted dungeons with copy pasted bosses. There's too many crannies to search and vast open areas with nothing of note. When you do find an item hidden out in the open world, 9 times out of 10 it's a leaf or a mushroom. You are not rewarded nearly enough for going down optional paths and that's a problem for a game as big as Elden Ring. The bosses are more aggressive than ever before and there needs to be a line. Bosses have these seemingly endless combos with lots of forward momentum. You'll get a VERY small window of opportunity to hit the boss like once or twice, then it's back to these ridiculously long combos. You barely get to attack, it's just roll city and if you get caught, a third or more of your HP is gone. And my last complaint is that this game is waaaaay too long for a souls game. Part of the fun of these games is that the run time is long enough to be significant but short enough to where you want to go through it again with a new weapon/build. In Elden Ring I was exhausted by the time the credits rolled and I didn't want to try out any cool new builds. Such a shame.

items.quote: (The Lands Between)، يمكنني القول بثقة أن Elden Ring ليست مجرد لعبة أخرى من استوديو FromSoftware، بل هي ذروة ما وصل إليه تصميم الألعاب في العقد الأخير. نجح المطور "هيديتاكا ميازاكي" بالتعاون مع الكاتب "جورج ر. ر. مارتن" في خلق عالم يجمع بين الغموض، القسوة، والجمال الساحر.1. العالم المفتوح والتصميم (World Design):أكبر إنجاز في هذه اللعبة هو كيف تعاملت مع مفهوم "العالم المفتوح". على عكس الألعاب الأخرى التي تملأ الخريطة بنقاط ومهام تكرارية، تمنحك Elden Ring حرية مطلقة بدافع الفضول فقط. كل قلعة تراها في الأفق يمكنك الوصول إليها، وكل كهف مظلم يخبئ خلفه زعيماً فريداً أو سلاحاً أسطورياً. الخريطة ليست مجرد مساحة شاسعة، بل هي طبقات من الأسرار التي لا تنتهي.2. أسلوب اللعب والتحدي (Gameplay & Combat):حافظت اللعبة على الحمض النووي لسلسلة "سولز"، لكنها أضافت أبعاداً جديدة. نظام القتال بالسيوف أو السحر أصبح أكثر سلاسة، وإضافة "الرماد المفقود" (Ashes of War) أعطت اللاعبين تخصيصاً غير مسبوق للأسلحة. كما أن إضافة "المتوج" (Torrent) للركوب جعلت التنقل والقتال فوق الحصان تجربة حماسية وتكتيكية.التحدي لا يزال حاضراً وبقوة، لكن اللعبة الآن أكثر "إنصافاً"؛ فإذا واجهت زعيماً صعباً، يمكنك ببساطة الذهاب لاستكشاف منطقة أخرى، تقوية شخصيتك، ثم العودة لاحقاً، وهذا يقلل من حاجز الإحباط الذي قد يواجهه اللاعبون الجدد.3. التوجه الفني والموسيقى (Art Direction & Sound):من الناحية البصرية، اللعبة لوحة فنية متحركة. تصميم الأعداء والزعماء مرعب ومبهر في آن واحد. أما الموسيقى، فهي عنصر أساسي في بناء الملحمية، خاصة في مواجهات الزعماء الكبار، حيث ترفع من وتيرة الأدرينالين وتجعلك تشعر بعظمة الموقف.4. القصة والسرد (Lore & Narrative):أسلوب السرد لا يزال يعتمد على "الغموض البيئي" وقراءة أوصاف الأدوات، وهو ما يعطي متعة خاصة لمن يحب تحليل القصص وبناء النظريات. تعاون جورج مارتن واضح في بناء التاريخ العميق للعالم والصراعات بين العائلات الحاكمة، مما أعطى العالم ثقلاً درامياً كبيراً.الخلاصة:Elden Ring هي تجربة نادرة الحدوث. إنها لعبة تحترم ذكاء اللاعب ولا تمسك يده طوال الوقت، بل تدفعه لاستكشاف المجهول ومواجهة مخاوفه. سواء كنت من عشاق ألعاب السولز القدامى أو لاعباً جديداً يبحث عن مغامرة لا تُنسى، فإن هذه اللعبة هي الخيار الأمثل. إنها "المعيار الذهبي" الجديد لما يجب أن يكون عليه العالم المفتوح.

items.quote:
Elden Ring is one of those rare games that actually feels like a leap forward in its genre. FromSoftware and George R. R. Martin created a beautiful world, even if the story is hidden behind item descriptions, the fact that the world blends the signature combat that Dark Souls is known for with an amazing open world just works so well. 

What really stood out to me when playing was the sense of freedom that the game hands you. You have a quest to follow but the game doesn't really restrict you to it. It feels like it's more about exploring and discovering new things, I'm on my like 10th character and still find things I didn't know about. 

The gameplay is classic FromSoftware. It's a tough game but it's fair, most of the time, requiring patience, timing, and strategy. The fact you can build your character however you want is great. One run you might be a samurai, the next a wizard, or you could end up being a giant tank build with a hammer one shotting everything you come into contact with and it's always fun to see how I want to play the game with a new character, though I seem to always drift to the moonlight great sword.

All this praise but being realistic no game is perfect. The game can feel overwhelming for newcomers at times. There are moments where the difficulty can spike or a lack of direction leads to confusion especially in side quests.  

Overall the game is amazing and offers an unforgettable experience that pushes the boundaries of open world games. I highly recommend this to players of RPGs and people who enjoy dark fantasy. Personal favorite boss is dragon lord placidusax as it's an epic fight.

items.quote:
Elden Ring: A Masterclass in Atmospheric Discovery
Nearly four years since its debut, Elden Ring remains the gold standard for open-world design. It isn't just a "Dark Souls with a horse"; it’s a radical reimagining of how curiosity should be rewarded in a video game.
The World: The Lands Between
The genius of Elden Ring lies in its organic exploration. Unlike many open-world titles that clutter your screen with icons and "to-do" lists, Elden Ring trusts the player.
Visual Storytelling: You see a distant, glowing tree or a crumbling castle on a cliff, and you simply go there.  
The Scale: Just when you think you’ve seen the map, you find an elevator that takes you to a sprawling underground starry city, or a hidden portal to a crumbling sky temple.
Atmosphere: The collaboration between Hidetaka Miyazaki and George R.R. Martin creates a world that feels ancient, tragic, and indifferent to your existence.

items.quote: Elden Ring is an incredibly vast game, defined by a level of freedom that feels almost limitless. Beyond simply being open-world, it is built on the foundation of absolute player freedom. From the way your character looks to how they fight, the depth of customization is remarkable. It allows you to express your own playstyle and identity without ever compromising the game’s core essence or its challenging **** game naturally encourages replayability, reminding me of roguelike experiences without actually being one. Every playthrough feels unique, not just because of different builds, but because of the freedom in how you approach the world itself. This gives the game a strong sense of personality that goes beyond just exploration.Elden Ring expands your mind in a way few games do. Its aesthetic, its gameplay design, and its philosophical and abstract concepts including its Lovecraftian elements create an experience that feels both mysterious and deeply complex. Its story, while intricate and sometimes difficult to fully grasp, is undeniably impressive and rewarding.Without a doubt, I consider Elden Ring to be the greatest work of art I have personally experienced in gaming. It is truly life-changing, and I genuinely believe it is an essential experience that no one should miss.

items.quote:
Elden Ring is easily one of the best games I have ever played.

It brings fun combat, some of the best open world gameplay and exploration, lots of build variety, crazy lore and writing, an incredible OST, beautiful artstyle and atmosphere, a charming multiplayer system, and great replaybility, all in FromSoftware's unique gameplay design.

If you are a fan of any FromSoftware game, open world games, action games or RPGs, this game should be an instant buy for you.

FromSoft games always have a unique design to them, and Elden Ring isn't much different; it's a hard game, the player has to learn it, however Elden Ring provides a lot more options to the player now due to it's open world nature, making it more accessible to weaker players, yet retaining the option for harder gameplay to veteran players.

This game should be a must-play to anyone who enjoys video games.

items.quote:
Over four years since release and the game does not get old. 
Art direction is gorgeous and still one of the best in any game to date. A ridiculous amount of builds to go with due to the vast scale of weapons and customisation with ashes of war and smithing stones- Want to have a colossal great sword on a strength build and still have the ability to use a side dagger/curved sword with parry? You can do that. Want to use a heavy shield and a thrusting sword and use magic? to whittle enemies down? Yep, that, too.

Replayability on this game is almost endless - you can farm runes quite easily late game and max out tonnes of weapons at your leisure , experimenting with different builds and weapons and going to fight other players either in 1v1s or invading. Almost every playthrough you will find something you didn't in the previous due to the scale of the map and easily missing areas, caves etc. So much to explore and find.

My first FS game was Bloodborne in 2018, then played Demon's Souls followed by the DS trilogy. Let me say this: I think anyone who says the original Dark Souls games that came before this are better, really are kidding themselves or are trying to be contrarian hipsters. This game does everything they all do but better and broader.

The game is a masterpiece in every sense.

items.quote: Don't let the number of amazing reviews and ratings fool you. Elden Ring is the worst AAA game you will probably ever play. From Software went from an intricate and connected crafted world to a very boring and poorly designed open world game. The open world does allow you access some items early if you know where it's at but is a complete downgrade besides that. You just ride around on your horse looking for ruins sticking out of the ground to go down stairs and open a door to get an item. Sometimes there is a boss as well. Most of the gameplay comes from the "dungeons" which are just holes in the side of mountains that come in the form of caves, mines, and catacombs. The worst part is the tracking on every enemy attack is so broken that actually dodging is almost impossible even if you know the ambush is there. A lot of attacks have phantom range as well in the form of shockwaves. Enemies change the direction of their jump in midair to hit you even if you shouldn't have been. A lot of enemies will even randomly slide forward so there attacks don't miss. The open world does cause a quantity over quality problem too. You see the same enemies and bosses way to many times throughout the game. Almost everything about this game is designed to make you as miserable as possible and pretend it's difficult instead of unfair. They added a jump button but there is a lot of precision platforming and jumps that you can just barely make. Even the drop rates are garbage and you can farm an enemy for hours to get one item.  Enemies and bosses move and attack in unnatural ways and have an overwhelming physical advantage over you and what your character is capable of. There is have barely any delay between combos allowing you any chance to fight back. They also react to your actions and dodge your actions and rush you when you heal as well. Their distance closing abilities are so good that range isn't really an option. All From Software had to do was leave the bosses the way they were in dark souls 3 which were the best part of that game. Any balance or positive mechanics from older From Software is long gone. You are pretty much forced into faster builds if playing by yourself. There are npc summons called spirit ashes but they are of limited use. If they could be summoned at any time the game would be much more manageable. They fall off horribly in new game plus and in the dlc so that would still only be a bandaid. A lot of boss battles have multiple bosses at the same time so playing the game without any help is nearly impossible. From software also punished you with bs like button press memory and attacks bouncing off walls while enemies go through them because you can't be disadvantaged enough for them. If you played Dark Souls 3 you know they made the enemies faster so magic was so slow it was useless and this game made the problem even worse. Weapons for intelligence, faith and arcane builds are hard to come by early on as well and the whet blades to infuse weapons with those stat scaling are even farther in the game. The actual sorceries and incantations are very imbalanced as well. Some of them take up to three spell slots and are incredibly underpowered. Bigger weapons can be too slow to even swing between enemy combos which is ridiculous. From Software loves to nerf things that are actually good and add detrimental effects like taking increased damage to make things unusable. Even the positive bonuses are negligible compared to older games accessories like a 8 percent increase to something instead of 20 percent . Later in the game everything is even worse as everyone has boss levels of health and can easily two shot you with high vigor stat.  I honestly don't see how anyone can find the game fun or enjoyable since everything in it is designed to make it artificially difficult and antifun because that is what From Software is known for. Elden Ring is proof they don't take praise or criticism of their games seriously. I can't imagine future games from this developer will be any better either. I guess it doesn't matter since the game got so many underserved glowing reviews and game of the year. It has as much hatred for the reasons I listed as praise by "hardcore gamers" who love to brag about how good they are at video games like it matters to anyone else. I think professional game reviewers are more concerned with job security and not burning bridges with companies than doing their jobs. The main type of players for these "souls like" games are notorious for being arrogant and elitist too. The game had a lot of potential but it's redeeming qualities are completely overshadowed by it's overwhelmingly bad gameplay experience. I guess PvP might not be too bad since other players are the only ones who don't "anime" all over the place while you stand there desperately flailing against whatever you are fighting. Hopefully From SoftWares next games don't sale well so they might actually care about what players want.

This is another "soulsgame" by the inventor of soulsgames. 
Not more, not less.
If you liked previous Fromsoft Games, you'll very likely enjoy this one, too. 
Openworld-Design is good, artdesign too, I'd say the artdesign is Fromsoft's strenght in general. At least for me it's the reason to play their games.

items.quote: So I just got done replaying Elden Ring and this time I did all the DLC and everything and all the side stuff, and I'm certain now, this is the best video game ever made, like objectively. I've been a fan of the From Software soulslikes for years now and after replaying them all recently my big take away is that they just get better at what they do with every game they make. And that's saying something because even Demon's Souls is a fantastic game, but Elden Ring? Elden Ring is the pinnacle, the very best of everything video games has come to offer us up to this point. Like think about the people that were making the very first video games, those text only dungeon crawlers and stuff like that - those people's wildest dreams for the future probably looked a lot like this game. What really sets it apart more than anything else is the open world - there's just no other open world in any other game ever that holds the same level of mystery to it. I mean once you're out there for the first time and you can walk in any direction and get into something absolutely fascinating at every turn, there just is no other game that has captured that other than maybe Breath of the Wild. But then you add in this brutal learning curve with the combat and the boss fights, and now you're in a situation where you have to earn the spoils from whatever you discover out there, and that's a combination that has yet to be duplicated. When I think about the most important, most influential video games of all time, I think about games like Super Mario Brothers 3, Punch Out, Final Fantasy VII, and other games where you can see their influence everywhere. And to be clear I don't think Elden Ring is in that category yet, but only because not enough time has passed, it'll be there in 10 years, no doubt. But when I think of what the best game ever is, personally I think less about it's level of influence and more about how well it would represent gaming as a whole to an outsider. Like if we were gonna put a video game in a time capsule and shoot it out into space for aliens to find, like we're putting Elden Ring in that thing, right? What else could possibly be a better choice? The only argument I can see against it being the best of all time is that it is pretty difficult if you're not a veteran of the genre, so you could make the point that the very best representation of gaming would be more accessible. But I think there's an equally good counterpoint there - I mean do we really think the best virtual adventure of all time should be something that anyone could do? A lot of the satisfaction of the journey comes from overcoming intense hardship, right? And that's an excellent way to describe some of these boss fights - extremely intense hardship.

items.quote:
在认真思考之下，我决定给艾尔登法环8分，作为对比，我给了只狼和塞尔达9分。由于艾尔登法环超高的评分，无上的口碑，诸多的优点我也不再赘述，本文主要讲讲为什么我无法给出更高的分数，为什么有的玩家并没有狂热地喜欢法环。我会从各个方面聊聊我的看法，仅代表个人观点。下面内容涉及大量【剧透】。

在我看来，在诸多的艺术品类中，这样的开放世界RPG游戏更接近于电影和戏剧，并在此之上极大地增加了以玩家为主的互动性。对我而言，我非常在意一个故事的情节、内核、表达。我作为玩家之互动参与，也应该极大地融入于这个故事。
以这个为标准，艾尔登法环是个中庸的游戏。它带来了庞大的全新的世界观，但是没有带来这个新世界下立体的人物和精彩的故事。我在最后毫不犹豫地召唤了菈妮作为我的结局，很大程度上是因为菈妮线是这个游戏中指引最明确，人物形象、性格最鲜明，最让我有代入感的。我在游玩的时候，始终不知道为何女王消失，为何法环破碎，我又为何要死要活地去修复它，无上意志和双指都是哪来的。我都打完女武神了，米莉森还站在亚坛，因为她嘴上说要见女武神，实际上是要日荫城的义手。至于诸多的Boss和NPC们到底谁是谁的孩子，我甚至到今天都能在网上看到人们争论。如果不在b站看几个讲述法环世界观的视频，根本就不明白这个游戏在讲什么，而即使看完了所有的剧情分析，也觉得索然无味，不过如此。
那人们可能就要说了，很多游戏的故事和内容都写在物品的介绍里面，我没有看。我对此是不能否认的，但也有这么几个问题：1. 这个游戏本来就充满谜语人，再加上非常低水平的简体中文翻译，很多东西我即使看了也不是很明白。晦涩的概念往往很难在脑海中记住，想必参加过高考的人们应该感同身受；2. 如果我没有这个物品呢？开放世界的意义难道必须且强制的在于玩家地毯式的搜索吗？事实上在我等级变高，玩法流派成型之后，我反而缺少了通过探索找到新物品提升角色的动力：绝大多数的物品都与我的流派无关，边角料永远都不是影响剧情的重要物品。再加上极其重复的墓地、废墟、矿坑，王城过了之后真的就没有任何探索的动力了，只想早点下一个boss看新剧情看结局。
总而言之，这种极弱指引+无任务日志+非常用汉语+碎片叙事的究极结果，就是我认为这个游戏的故事很差劲。网上诸多将法环捧上天的资深魂游玩家，往往也聚焦于其他方面。

那么第二点，我们聊聊大家最常说的美术。我认为整体上来说环境的美术还是不错的，很多场景都让我印象深刻，十分震撼：第一次下地下，利耶尼亚辉石龙超大范围的蓝火+允许骑马战斗，满月女王的场景，碎星的场景，第一次来到亚坛高原，第一次上月光高地，从赐福点走出来看到俯视王城。不过我也要指出，亚坛高原之前的地区往往饱和度过低，这有两个结果：1. 配合非常无聊的音乐，乱跑式的自由探索并不是很有意思；2. 很多关键的人物、道具与环境融为一体。事实上，“路过赐福点没发现，路边有NPC没注意”这种事情我常有发生。在类似壶哥的声音指引之外，其实可以让NPC原地踱步，或者增加一些动作，甚至直接修改NPC的亮度、衣服颜色、饱和度的设计，其实对指引是巨大的帮助。另外，人物形象的设计大量带有头部饰品，面部细节的缺失+没有任何动作也影响了人物形象的塑造，我认为在一些设计好的动画之外，关键的对话也需要推一个NPC近景的镜头来增强氛围感。

接下来就是音乐，除了游戏初始菜单界面的主题曲（亦是皮蛋的BGM），其他的音乐我觉得非常一般，没有让我印象深刻的曲子，没有让我在流媒体平台收藏原声轨的冲动，无数的b站的视频解说和教程配着塞尔达的BGM。我相信更好的音乐能极大地渲染类似于王城、天空城、地下的氛围。能让游戏进入到后期形成与前期显著不同的节奏和对比，能缓解玩家后期探索的疲惫程度。

最后说说作为动作游戏的游戏性。首先是手柄按键，很多游戏的轻攻击都是X，然而这边是RB。奔跑跟闪避键绑定，我为了方便奔跑直接改到了RT，但是也进一步增加了已经非常高的闪避延迟。地图设计上，有仇恨的情况下不能开地图（完全可以禁传送但是允许开地图）。有太多的墙角和陷阱都是重复的，玩到后期就觉得为了恶心我而恶心我。不过我其实挺喜欢跳跳乐的。数值设计得很复杂，但是根本看不见，所谓增加攻击力、增加威力，到底增加多少，一概没有。我感觉任何关于战术甚至猴戏的设计都依赖于在网上查数值以及研究不同buff之间的冲突情况。

可能出人意料，我对这个游戏最大的建议其实是把体量减小一点，我一周目不含DLC110小时大概180级，就这样还有三四个墓地没有探。我至今认为50小时只狼带给我的震撼回忆远超过刺客信条英灵殿的100小时LGBT之旅。我确实欣赏史东薇尔和王城的箱庭设计，可火山和天空城真没太多意思。量大分足从来不是什么卖点，馒头也量很大，但是不值钱。不要为了胚胎的地图形状强行把雪山做大，减少重复的boss使用，泥头车创一次真就足够了。我其实觉得量小一点更能保持新鲜感，玩家总有意犹未尽的感觉，而不是游戏时长过长带来的审美疲劳。

在我难得的假期花上将近4周的时间，我会说总体还是值得的，再有时间之后的DLC也会考虑游玩，这也是我给出8分的理由。法环的价格也并不是离谱的高，销量也非常好看。然而这绝无可能成为我心中游戏历史长河的最高神作，也绝无可能是我推荐给未来女朋友开拓新爱好的敲门砖。

items.quote:
This game is such a refresher from the other typical AAA games, where the game tells you where to go and holds your hand. Here you can go wherever you want and do the main stuff whenever you want. The player can find interesting mechanics and different ways to play the game. Every playthrough is different and game is very replayable.

The game is beautiful, the architecture is detailed and enormous. definitely the best looking game I have ever played.

There are many different bosses with different attacks and gimmicks. Their design is cool. You can use many different weapons to defeat them, depending on how the player wants to play.

In my opinion the game is not 'hard'. You can get items, that make your journey easier. But the game can be very very annoying. There is a fine line between hard and annoying bosses. Attacks, which take 5 seconds to happen without any signal that the boss will suddenly swing his weapon for example are just bad game design. If you can see with your eyes when the boss will hit then it is not a problem, but if it is very sudden then it is just not fun. Also attacks that one shot you are most of the time unnecessary. If the boss only has one it's ok but more than that is very annoying. The fact that the game doesn't tell u some things can also be a bad thing. What do you mean there are fake walls and some riddles are basically impossible without guides. That's why I am not giving a 10/10.

Overall the game is very impressive and everyone should give it a try, but sometimes you will want throw your controller and uninstall the game, but this will probably be just a temporary state.

items.author: MaomettoNino

items.quote: Elden Ring is one of the greatest – if not the best – games of all time. Yes, it may have some flaws in its graphics; however, the greatness of the game makes you ignore them entirely. Everything there is to say about Elden Ring feels perfect.First of all, the art direction is absolutely gorgeous. And even though, as I said before, there are some performance issues, the artistic design is so impressive that it makes the whole game feel almost alien.Then there is the structure of the open world. No more bland, massive worlds where a symbol guides you wherever you go. In this game, every region has its own story, its own meaning, and its own very intriguing side quests — the kind you genuinely want to finish — all without any hand-holding from the game.Furthermore, the music is magnificent, blending perfectly with the environment. From the boss themes to the “background’’ music of the open world, everything feels like a treasure to your ears.Moreover, the gameplay is like a form of precise surgery. It may feel simple at first, but it’s not. Every puzzle, every boss, and even every minor enemy has different mechanics that you must adapt to.I mentioned the bosses earlier, but I feel they deserve to be mentioned again just to emphasize how well-constructed they are. Yes, they may be difficult, but when you finally defeat them, you get the feeling that you’ve accomplished something truly important.Last but not least, the lore of the game is one of the best-written stories ever. It has so much depth that it stands alongside other genre-defining worlds such as The Lord of the Rings — especially after George R. R. Martin’s **** in all, this game definitely deserves your time and cannot be overlooked. I have played many great games, but this one remains my favorite.

items.quote: Elden Ring can be highly praised for recreating the sense of exploration that Dark Souls 1 offered. Although the latter portions of the game feel somewhat less dense, the impressive boss designs and overall scale of the experience more than make up for it.

items.quote:
ゲームは傑作だが、一部コミュニティの異常な攻撃性には注意が必要です

ゲーム自体は本当に素晴らしい作品です。しかし、プレイヤーコミュニティの一部には、通常の“対人ゲーのノリ”では済まされない、極端な攻撃性と粘着性が存在します。

私は数年にわたり、SNSや匿名掲示板でハンドル名・IDを追跡され、長期にわたる誹謗中傷・侮辱・個人情報の拡散・虚偽のストーリー拡散といった被害を受けました。周囲の関係者にも被害が及び、通院を余儀なくされた人間もいます。

この行為が単なる「ネットの悪ふざけ」ではなく、明確な違法行為に該当すると判断し、
弁護士を通じて刑事告訴の手続きを開始しました。
すでに警察・運営には証拠を提出済みで、現在進行中です。

もちろん、すべてのプレイヤーがこのような行動をするわけではありません。
しかし、特定のコミュニティでは、標的を決めた“数年単位の集団粘着”が発生し、
初心者や孤立しやすいプレイヤーが被害を受けやすい状況が実際に存在します。

ゲームは本当に素晴らしい。
ですが、オンライン関連のコミュニティに参加する際はくれぐれも慎重に,
個人情報やIDを広範囲に公開しないことを強くおすすめします。

同じような被害者がこれ以上増えないことを心から願っています。

Não sei nem por onde começo a falar dos pontos negativos, mas o jogo é extremamente mau otimizado (tem gráficos de ps3 e mesmo assim não consegue manter 60 fps nem no ps5), extremamente repetitivo (mais de 100 boss fights repetidas, isso quando não são apenas mobs aleatórios do mapa com barra de vida de boss), as quests são mto vagas,o jogo é pouquíssimo elucidante quanto aos objetivos e também as quests são bastante repetitivas (sempre tendo que matar invasores). items.quote: Elden Ring is truly one of the best open world RPGs that allows the player to traverse a vast and awe-inspiring world that perfectly presents the entire dark fantasy subgenre, allowing the player to freely explore such a stunning and frightening world with many secrets to discover. It takes its past games flaws and builds upon them making the game feel much more polished and fresher compared to its counter parts. The large amount of exploration keeps the player immersed in Miyazaki’s imagination and allows them to play it at their own pace. The combat feels rewarding as you dive further into the game itself, creating a serene but exciting sense of achievement after fuelling and testing the player’s determination. Its OST perfectly sets the tone and mood for certain areas, if that's in a cave, a castle or just in an open area, it makes the player feel constantly engrossed in its environments along with the intimidating music for its major storyline enemies. Overall, the repetitiveness of the game shows an exponential change in the player’s abilities and understanding on certain challenges they must overcome, allowing them to adapt and improve against different enemies. By the end of the game, it will leave you awe struck just by the sheer beauty of the scenery and the journey you took to get to that point, leaving the feeling of immense pride and success in the player. It is truly one of the few games that will go down in history.

items.quote: As someone who’s sunk countless hours into Soulsborne titles—from Demon’s Souls to Sekiro—I can confidently say Elden Ring is FromSoftware’s magnum opus. It’s not just a culmination of everything they’ve learned over the years; it’s a game that gives players the freedom to truly make the experience their own.What makes Elden Ring special is how naturally it adapts to your playstyle. Whether you prefer the methodical patience **** user, the precision of a dex build, or the chaos of magic and summons, the game never punishes you for how you want to play—it challenges you to refine it. Every encounter feels like a test, not of reflexes alone, but of creativity and ****’s undeniably tough—there are moments of pure frustration where a boss feels insurmountable—but when you finally overcome that wall, the sense of satisfaction is unmatched. What’s even more impressive is how that challenge never feels artificial. The world itself teaches you, shaping your instincts until you start reading patterns, predicting movements, and mastering the flow of combat almost without realizing it.Exploration is where Elden Ring truly shines. The pacing is near perfect: long stretches of quiet discovery punctuated by moments of awe or terror. You’ll spend hours wandering, following a hunch or a distant light on the horizon, and every path somehow leads to something worthwhile—be it a hidden boss, a mysterious NPC, or a breathtaking view that makes you pause just to take it in.Time slips away easily here. One minute you’re clearing out a dungeon; the next, you’ve lost an entire evening exploring a single region. Yet it never feels like a grind—just a steady, natural rhythm of curiosity and reward.Every path you take eventually loops back into something greater, connecting stories, regions, and revelations in ways that only become clear after dozens of hours. And when those pieces finally click into place, it’s hard not to sit back and appreciate just how intricately designed this world **** the end, Elden Ring isn’t just challenging or beautiful—it’s alive. It’s a game that respects the player enough to let them forge their own journey, with all the triumphs, losses, and discoveries that come with it. Simply put: it’s one of the most fulfilling experiences gaming has to offer.

items.quote:
Elden Ring is the biggest and in my opinion best game that the Fromsoftware team have produced at the time of writing. The world is huge and filled with deep lore and fun combat encounters.

GAMEPLAY: 10/10 - I personally love the "Soulsborne" combat style and this game is the most fleshed out and smooth version to date.

STORY: 9/10 - While the story of Elden Ring is incredibly deep and detailed and just all round amazing, I cannot give it any higher than a 9 simply due to the fact that most players will come away from the game not understanding much at all about the story unless they spent hours reading item descriptions and doing every hidden questline. I like this style of storytelling but it leaves a lot of players in the dark.

SOUNDTRACK: 9/10 - While the soundtrack of this game is epic and orchestrated very well, very few of the songs stick out as especially memorable besides the main theme played on the title screen.

CHARACTERS: 9/10 - Almost all of the characters are interesting and are voice acted very well, and a lot have long side quests that have you feel even more invested in the characters.

GRAPHICS/VISUALS: 10/10 - While the pure graphics in Elden Ring aren't bad they aren't anything special. However, the art direction and colour theory used throughout the game makes the game look simply magical. As long as you don't look too closely at individual textures, Elden Ring is one of if not the most beautiful game out at the moment.

CUTSCENES: 10/10 - There are very few cutscenes in Elden Ring, but when one does play you know you are in for a treat. All cutscenes serve their purpose incredibly well, whether it's introducing a new intimidating boss or telling you lore before the game starts. 

Overall, Elden Ring is an incredible game and even if you disregard the story entirely (which you shouldn't) is an incredibly fun and challenging game. If the Fromsoftware team continue on this trajectory for their next mainline game, we are all in for a treat.

items.quote:
Elden Ring brings so much to the table that the table almost breaks.

Elden Ring, the seventh scion of the noble Soulsborne house, has quite a legacy to live up to. As the popular siblings tend to do, it surpasses all these expectations with seeming ease and looks splendid doing it, too.That is not a metaphor. The production values of this game are through the roof, as everyone stepping even one foot into the Lands Between will attest. The Great Outdoors greets its intrepid explorers with incredibly lush vegetation, a masterpiece of a sky box, majestic mountains, foreboding castles and a golden haze of light beatifying everything. Where earlier Soulsborne titles used to trap their players in incredibly intricate labyrinths, Elden Ring sets you loose in a gigantic open world and tells you to go nuts. Every single place you can see on the horizon you can set a food in, and in a few other places you would never suspect are there besides. Just take note of the golden knight over there. He will in all probability cut you down a few times, just to start things off on the right foot.

Whether you make your first experience in combat with him or the much softer targets beyond him, combat feels very familiar to a Dark Souls 3 veteran. A couple of things have been added: A jump button complete with jump attacks, a horse to get around on and engage in mounted combat, and probably the most consequential addition: Spirit summons, the ability to conjure up an NPC to fight with you in certain situations, e. g. boss fights.

When encountering this feature, the brows of an experienced Dark Souls player furrow. Won’t this mess with the hallowed Difficulty, make things way too easy?

To my mind, it does only a little. Elden Ring is an appropriately harsh game: If you play it like a traditional Souls game, it will send you to the death screen quite often. But it is the kind of dominatrix that really is in it mainly for your enjoyment: The kind who always makes sure that the straps have cushy insides, who always sets down a pillow under the pillory, who always listens an extra second for your safe word before proceeding. Whether it is a particularly difficult constellation of regular enemies or one of the dozens of stunning and exciting boss fights that have you stumped, somewhere out there is a spell, a weapon or a spirit companion that will help you jump that hurdle and still feel like a bad-ass for having done so. Or you can do it the old-fashioned way and just bang your head against the wall until the wall is reduced to rubble. You do you. Just one problem: If you do want that vintage Dark Souls experience, you have to resist the siren call of the spirit summons, not just once, but every time a boss has struck you down with only one percent of health remaining. That might be a tall order.

But all this quibbling about difficulty aside, combat is still an eternal font of enjoyment. Squaring off against a Cleanrot Knight is just as enjoyable in hour 200 as fighting a lowly foot soldier was in hour 1. The core gameplay loop of Elden Ring is second to none.

One area where there has been remarkable progress in the Soulsborne franchise is the story telling. That doesn’t mean that the plot told is any less cryptic than before, but it is told in considerably less impenetrable fashion. There are quest chains that one might even be able to solve without resorting to the wiki! Some of them are quite engaging too, even if most of them end up on the grimdark side of the spectrum. So the plot department hasn't exactly delivered a diamond of storytelling, but they have polished their part of the grand opus a lot more than they used to do.

Still, the story isn’t the draw of a Soulsborne game, and Elden Ring is no exception. Fighting for your life in spectacular yet grounded fashion in high stakes high difficulty duels with superbly animated foes in front of spectacularly beautiful vistas is. In these regards, Elden Ring delivers in spades. So much so in fact that it was almost too much for me. The Lands Between are vast, and if you truly mean to see and do everything, you are looking at a 200 hour time commitment, at least. That amount of time can be hard to come by, and sustaining sufficient amounts of enthusiasm for this long a time can be a challenge, no matter how enticing the game might be.

But whatever amount of time you choose to let Elden Ring embrace you, you will have an excellent experience full of wonder, existential dread, mortal danger, frustration, elation, and always a new thing to discover right around the corner. Every session of Elden Ring truly feels like an adventure.

TLDR: Elden Ring is the pinnacle of polish in the Soulslike genre: welcoming to all players, appropriately harsh to the fans. Almost too much ****, maybe, but an excellent experience for whatever amount of time you choose to give it.

items.quote:
Introduction
Elden Ring is not just another game—it’s an experience. For years, I avoided Souls games after a short and frustrating attempt at Dark Souls when I was younger. The mechanics felt alien, the difficulty overwhelming. But years later, curiosity brought me back when I saw the overwhelming praise for Elden Ring. This became my first true Souls-like adventure, and to my surprise, it was absolutely worth it.
Story & World
The story of Elden Ring is deep, mysterious, and often intentionally confusing. On the surface, your path is clear: rise as the Tarnished and seek to become Elden Lord. But underneath, every character you meet, every death you face, has meaning. Even your own repeated deaths are explained within the lore.That said, following the narrative in your first playthrough can be tough. Characters appear based on the order in which you explore, which can jumble the story. On my first run, I defeated harder bosses before even stumbling upon one of the easier ones. After three completions, I finally watched a two-hour lore breakdown online—and only then did I truly appreciate how rich the story really is. For some players, this fragmented storytelling may feel like nonsense, but for others, it’s part of the magic.
Gameplay
This is where Elden Ring shines brightest. At its core, the controls are simple: light attacks, heavy attacks, parrying, dodging, and ranged aiming. But the true depth lies in the staggering amount of equipment—over 300 weapons and 500 armor sets—each dramatically changing your playstyle. Combine that with attributes, consumables, and upgrades, and you’re looking at endless possibilities to reinvent your build.Boss battles are the beating heart of the game. Each boss is beautifully designed, both visually and mechanically, with unique attack patterns that force you to adapt and learn. The difficulty is real, but it’s also fair. Sometimes you’ll die a hundred times learning an encounter. Other times, with the right upgrades or a clever build, you might down a boss in one attempt. Either way, the victory always feels earned.Exploration in the open world adds another layer of freedom. Unlike earlier Souls games, you can escape frustrating dead ends by venturing elsewhere. If an area feels overwhelming, simply explore a different region, gather upgrades, and return stronger. The downside is that you can sometimes wander into overly difficult zones too early, which can cause burnout.
Visuals & Sound
From haunting ruins to breathtaking skies, Elden Ring’s visuals are meticulously crafted. Every tree, road, and structure feels alive with history. The world communicates despair and decay while hinting at a glorious past, and this duality is one of the game’s greatest artistic achievements.Sound design enhances the experience. Basic enemy noises are distinct but simple, while boss battles explode with music that feels both majestic and terrifying. Those orchestral scores make you instantly regret underestimating an enemy and set the tone for the epic struggle ahead.
Accessibility & Challenge
For newcomers to the Souls genre, Elden Ring can be brutal in the opening hours. I spent over ten hours swearing at a single boss, convinced I was stuck forever. But the truth is, the game offers multiple paths: grind, explore, upgrade—or keep dying until you master the fight. Both approaches are valid, and that stubborn persistence is rewarded with some of the most satisfying victories gaming can **** recommendation for first-time players: don’t hesitate to look up guides, builds, or even ask experienced friends for advice. The learning curve is steep, but once you get past those early walls, the game becomes endlessly rewarding.
Verdict
Elden Ring is not just a game—it’s an unforgettable experience. From its vast and mysterious world to its punishing yet addictive gameplay, it delivers on almost every front. It can frustrate, confuse, and exhaust you, but it also creates moments of triumph that few games can match.

items.quote:
While Elden Ring undeniably delivers a satisfying and dynamic combat system that rewards skill and experimentation, the overall experience is not without its flaws. One of the most glaring issues is the excessive repetition scattered throughout the game world. Many dungeons, enemies, and even bosses feel recycled, which gradually dulls the sense of discovery that an open-world game should foster.

Another major drawback lies in the storytelling. The narrative is heavily obscured, relying too much on item descriptions and vague NPC dialogue. As a result, the emotional impact of the story is significantly weakened. I found myself disengaged from the characters and plot, eventually turning to YouTube just to grasp what the game was trying to convey. That’s not storytelling — that’s homework.

In summary, while Elden Ring excels in moment-to-moment gameplay, it struggles with repetition and a story that fails to connect on its own terms.

items.quote:
It was my first Soulsborne. For Fromsoft veterans maybe everything is good and on the bright side. I have mixed feelings and I start with the positive.
Most of the bosses are epic and well designed. They look so cool and if you manage to beat them, especially after they seemed impossible in the begginning, it feels like a big achievement. That feeling of accomplishement isn't in any other game. 
Although the graphics aren't totally next gen, the world is still nice and there is such a special gloomy atmosphere. Castles and other buildings are beautiful. There are a lot of items, consumables etc. (which isn't my favourite thing) but all those items aren't always needed to progress in the game and you don't have a limit to carry them with you, so it's fine and through that there's good variety of weapons. 
I'm a little disappointed of the exploration. Over 80% of times when I ran into a dungeon or something interesting, it wasn't worth the effort (except the runes, but you get those anyways if you're killing monsters). Can't rate the story because there is none, but I liked the few nice boss sequences. You have to get used to the controls but after 4-5 hours it's ok. The worst thing is the auto lock. So many times it just switches off and with bigger enemies like dragons or giants (in particular two main bosses) it's absolute chaos. Sometimes you are forced to grind to progress and there is no skill issue, I was underleveled for almost every boss fight which I won and there is only a level issue in this game. In this case you could call any game a soulslike, selecting the hardest difficulty, and just leveling up so that you don't get one shottet by enemies. Main and side quests are not clear, boring and there is no quest log. Just one of those things could have made life a lot easier. 
Overall it's cool and the challenge is so exciting (almost perfect). They have a few of the best bosses ever in video gaming. On the other hand the game has a few problems as mentioned that are totally overlooked by Fromsoft fans.

items.quote: Elden Ring is one of those complicated games where the things it does right surpass almost all of its contemporaries, but some game design decisions feel like a regression of its formula. This is after the DLC, Shadow of the Erdtree, which, while it wasn't bad, had negative elements that made me reevaluate every FromSoft game out there. Elden Ring's world is top notch, providing plenty of amazing opportunities that incentivize the player to find different things. It's a similar "Go anywhere and do anything" principle that made Breath of the Wild such a trailblazer, but Elden Ring's unique environments and art direction thanks to George R.R. Martin himself elevate that experience. Unfortunately, when it comes to exploration, a lot of it is gated behind the difficulty of enemies. And if that were just the case, then that would be alright since Fallout: New Vegas did something similar with its map design, but the issue is that the players of these games and the fundamental design of Souls games reward the player greatly for overcoming these challenges to the point that the "intended route" gated off by beginner enemies feels a little bit too trivial. While Souls games are infamous for not budging on their difficulty, not making these earlier areas harder for those that have overcome the rockier routes makes Elden Ring's pacing a little bit disappointing. Even Zelda did this back in 2017, where progression made harder variants of enemies spawn in earlier areas. Speaking of difficulty, the boss difficulty is challenging for sure, but it doesn't feel as fair as previous FromSoft games. There are more and more bosses in FromSoft games that pull out a crazy phase 2 attack that is basically impossible to predict based on its phase 1. There is hardly a natural progression of learning "the dance" between the phases, it's just a move to wipe your health out to create an illusion of "difficulty." This isn't every boss, it probably isn't even MOST of the bosses, but there is definitely an increasing number of them, and Shadow of the Erdtree exacerbated that issue. When all is said and done, though, this is just a concerning trend and some pretty minor things in the face of an excellent video game. While it isn't personally for me, it's still definitely a must-play for just about anybody.

items.quote:
️ Elden Ring – 10/10 ReviewPlatform Reviewed: PlayStation 5 / PC / Xbox Series XReviewer’s Score: ★★★★★★★★★★ (10/10)Elden Ring is a generational triumph — a masterclass in open-world design, atmosphere, and combat, crafted by FromSoftware at the peak of its creative power.From the moment you step into the Lands Between, Elden Ring overwhelms with its scale, beauty, and brutality. The world feels handcrafted yet massive, bleak yet full of wonder — each region distinct, teeming with secrets, lore, and challenge. Unlike many open-world games, exploration is never filler. Every cave, every ruin, every hill in the distance promises a meaningful discovery — whether it’s a legendary weapon or a horrifying monstrosity guarding it.Combat is surgical, deep, and endlessly customizable. Whether you’re a sword-wielding berserker, a tactical mage, or something in between, Elden Ring offers a playground for creative builds and experimentation. Boss fights are unforgettable — not just for their difficulty, but for their spectacle and design. These encounters demand mastery and reward patience, turning defeat into motivation rather than **** narrative — cryptic, environmental, and mythological — unfolds like a puzzle box. Written by Hidetaka Miyazaki with contributions from George R.R. Martin, the lore feels ancient, tragic, and deeply immersive. You don’t just play Elden Ring; you study it, unravel it.Technically, the game runs smoothly (especially post-patch), and its art direction — from decaying cathedrals to nightmarish swamps — is unmatched. The score is chilling and majestic, further enhancing the oppressive beauty of the world.
Elden Ring is not just one of the best games of the decade — it redefines what an open-world action RPG can be. It’s a brutal, beautiful odyssey that will be studied and imitated for years to come. If you play only one game this generation, make it this one.

The game is graphically gorgeous. I often found myself traversing the world just to see what was around the bend. That's kind of where my enjoyment ended though. I wasn't allowed to delight in leveling up, defeating bosses, or creating a great character build. **** game is far too punishing. The enemies in between destinations are spread out enough to be fun and challenging, and if you die, we'll it is easy enough to get back there to collect your dropped runes. But if you die in a location such as ruins, fortress or a cave/dungeon, the enemies are often overwhelming enough to take you down. Then you have to make it all the way back to where you bit the dust tore claim you dropped runes. Yes, you gotta walk back into the same hell hole that killed you **** what you lost the first time and it often kills you again causing you to lose your hard earned runes permanently. The controls are sluggish and the camera often is not dynamic enough to help you see your way out of trouble. The final nail in the coffin is the story, or lack thereof. There is not enough of it to grasp on to and make me understand why Im doing what Im doing, wandering around the vast, beautiful open world, or even really care. Your character is bland,the circumstances vague, and you wander aimlessly.

There are those this game was meant for. I was not one of them.

items.quote:
Note : 10/10
           100/100

Lorsqu'on s’y attend le moins, FromSoftware parvient une fois de plus à frapper fort. Elden Ring s’impose comme une œuvre magistrale, confirmant le savoir-faire du studio en matière de jeux d’action-RPG exigeants.

-Le monde ouvert, vaste, dense et rempli de secrets, a divisé une partie de la communauté. Certains lui ont reproché une forme de dispersion, voire une certaine répétitivité. Pour d’autres — et j’en fais partie — il s'agit au contraire d’une véritable prouesse de level design, où chaque recoin recèle une surprise, un défi ou un morceau de lore. Le gameplay atteint une maturité remarquable. 

-Fidèle à l’héritage des Dark Souls, Elden Ring conserve un système de combat fondé sur la précision et l’esquive, tout en enrichissant l’expérience avec une variété d’armes inédites, chacune dotée de mécaniques propres et d’un lore soigneusement intégré.

-Côté affrontements, les boss figurent parmi les meilleurs jamais conçus par FromSoftware. Leur mise en scène, leur difficulté et leur design contribuent à faire de chaque rencontre un moment mémorable. 

-La rejouabilité, renforcée par la richesse de l’exploration et la multiplicité des quêtes secondaires, est l’un des grands points forts du jeu.

-La difficulté, quant à elle, reste une caractéristique centrale. Toutefois, Elden Ring innove en offrant une courbe de progression plus flexible. En fonction de sa manière d’aborder le jeu — exploration approfondie, choix des équipements, invocation des esprits — l’expérience peut varier grandement. C’est un Souls qui s’adapte davantage à la manière de jouer du joueur, sans jamais trahir son exigence de base.

-En conclusion, Elden Ring est une œuvre monumentale. FromSoftware signe ici l’un des jeux les plus aboutis de sa carrière, et sans doute l’un des meilleurs open worlds jamais créés. Un véritable chef-d'œuvre du genre.

It's still locked to 60fps which is a no go for me. No PS5 controller support on PC as well (it works but you only see the XBOX signs, why??). Elden ring étant mon premier jeu de From Software j’ai commencé le jeu avec beaucoup d’appréhension en me demandent si je serais capable d’arriver à la fin du jeu. 
Et au final j’ai juste kiffé du début à la fin sur ce jeu qui est une véritable master class

Point positif

- Les combat son juste incroyablement kiffant, aussi dur que addictif, tout que sa soit les mobs normale ou les boss j’ai kiffé quasiment chaque combat. Et si les combats et surtout les boss sont aussi incroyable c’est grace au level design qui est juste dingue, incroyable véritable master classe a se niveau

- L’exploration c’est simple j’ai jamais pris autant de plaisir dans l’exploration d’un open world, le jeu récompense la curiosité de manière ludique, vous explorez un château et paf un portail vers une nouvelle zone incroyable , vous explorez un lac paf un boss magistral. Il a toujours une récompense quand vous explorez j’ai kiffé explorez le moindre cm de ce jeu

- L’univers est ultra riche: mystérieux, captivant et immersif de ouf

- La DA est a tomber par terre c’est juste un chef d’œuvre a se niveau la ,chaque niveau, lieu sont juste époustouflant de beauté

- Les musiques et la mise en scène des boss sont incroyable

- Une grande variété dans la manière de jouer vous pouvez jouer en force au corps a corps ou avec 2 armes en même temps ou encore avec de la magie. Cette liberté de gameplay est juste trop grisant

Point négatif

- Les boss sont incroyable mais malheureusement certains sont recyclés et du coup il perd leur coté unique

- J’ai eu plusieurs bug notamment avec la caméra mais rien de dramatique pour autant

- Parfois manque d’explication dans certains quêtes secondaires et surtout manque d’explication dans les menus, on comprend pas toujours a quoi sert telle objet et parfois on peut si perdre


Pour conclure Elden Ring est l’une de mes plus grandes surprises dans le jeu vidéo et un des jeux qui me marquera le plus, j’aurais pas cru au depart aimé se jeu a se point la. C’est un véritable chef d’œuvre a presque tout les niveaux et aussi certainement mon open world rpg préféré.

items.quote:
I played a total of 160 hours. So the game can't be bad. However, 40 hours of that is probably just playing bosses. Some of them took me a total of 3-4 hours to beat. The game is hard. However, the open world means you can choose your opponents. If you don't beat them, you go somewhere else. That's good. I spent the remaining hours walking through the world without knowing what to do or where to go. 

The combat and magic system is solid and fun. Switching items during a battle, on the other hand, is really difficult. As the enemies attack very quickly, you hardly have time to switch items fast enough. 

The main problem with Elden Ring for me is that it lacked variety. It's over 90 percent pure combat. No matter where you go, you fight. Everything wants to kill you, and you want to kill everything. Maybe 2% of the game is NPCs, conversations and story. For me, Elden Ring is not a role-playing game either. It's an action game with RPG elements.  If you enjoy fighting monsters, OK. If you compare Elden Ring with RPGs like Skyrim, Elex, Dragon Age etc., everything is missing: characters, story, plot, story. In Elden Ring you fight all the time and collect loot - and do almost nothing else. Apart from opponents, the world in Elden RIng is almost empty. Apart from the constant fighting, it's really boring.

The music is extremely boring, at least when exploring the world. A few tones that are constantly repeated. In Limgrave, the “music” is extremely annoying. But it's no better in other areas. The music is good during boss fights.

A big problem for me: Where are the quests? There are tasks, but the game gives you almost no indication of how the quest continues. I was constantly unsure of what to do, where to go, who of the few NPCs I should talk to. That's why I didn't finish the game in 160 hours and then gave up on Elden Ring. After that, I had no desire to even start the game again.

Conclusion: I had a lot of fun with the game for several weeks. The combat system is intense and difficult, but doable. But Elden Ring is tiring, often annoying and frustrating, the music is very bad overall, the plot is completely unclear, I don't understand the mission structure, there is a lack of characters and story.

Elden Ring is a game that I partly love and partly hate. I've never had it this extreme in a game before. That's why only 6 stars. I'll probably never turn the game on again because after this game I'm absolutely not in the mood for Elden Ring and Souls games anymore.

items.quote: Elden ring is a game that has largely renewed the soulslike RPG genre. It is one of the very few cases, if not perhaps the only one where a souls has an organized exploration in a vast open world structured in 5 main regions, each with a lore and various and interesting characteristics. items.quote:
A frustratingly great game, not only for how it makes you wonder if other developers are even trying, but also for how many annoying, tedious, frustrating, and unintuitive features are buried under an avalanche of insanely good moments. 
Elden Ring stands as one of the best open world games ever made for its uniquely brilliant and dark world, with so many memorable bosses and enemies populating it. It doesn't seem fair to compare it to other open world games like Zelda though - compared to BotW, Elden Ring is linear. This is instead more of a series of open zones, all with so many secrets and bosses to discover, and a lot of freedom in which areas you visit first. Ultimately, it is more restrictive than BotW, but it uses these restrictions to build a deliberate path through the world. There is nothing wrong with this sort of world design, but it is worth mentioning that it does not embody "freedom" as much as its contemporaries might. 
Elden Ring did borrow other elements from Zelda, however, including perhaps most importantly, freedom from hand-holding and explanation. You are truly left to discover this world, and it certainly has more content to uncover than a world like Hyrule. From the variety of different monsters and enemies, to the different items of a plethora of builds, the absurd array of weapons and spells, and countless interesting NPC's (with admittedly needlessly confusing and antiquated quests). There is always something to uncover in this game, and the settings are so brilliantly designed that you can't help but delve deep into all of them. The underground sections truly were some of the most insane moments I have had in any game, and the story that unravels as you venture through the regions left me genuinely fascinated. 
This game also borrows BotW's shrine dungeon approach, having many bite-sized challenges throughout the world, yet unlike BotW this game does not skip out on its legacy dungeons. Elden Ring has some of the most impressively designed cities and castles of any medium, which are all filled with a rich variety of enemies and bosses.
The bosses really are the highlight of this game, with countless standouts and memorable moments. Radahn was frustrating as hell, Margit was a crazy realisation of how bad I was at the game, The Crucible Knights were infuriating until I mastered them and then I realised how good they were, and of course we have Malenia, who is in fact the blade of I think Miquella, i think thats what she was yeah.
The bosses are fun and challenging, and I didn't mind the fact they were recycled, since the core combat system was so much fun that it didn't matter if I was fighting the same bosses again (except for Astel, that kind of ruined the original moment). 
The core combat of dodging and hitting is simple and serves as the core of all encounters, but the heavy and light attacks, ashes of war, parries, ranged attacks, consumables, jumps, and ripostes all add a heavy heap of variety. Not to mention the trillion and one build options from the unlimited number of weapons available. Every build is unique and every build is interesting. 
But that isn't necessarily a good thing. I prefer games with just one build, but the restrictive upgrade and leveling system makes experimentation hard anyways. Speaking of leveling, the different regions in this supposedly "open" world game have levels which soft lock areas for players until they gain more XP from fighting easier bosses on the critical path. Speaking of bosses, some of them are complete garbage and completely hopelessly unfair, or play by completely different rules than you.
This is a frustrating 10/10, and much of that frustration is the result of actual frustration from a combat system and collection of bosses that desperately needed a bit more polish and balancing. In a challenging game, you want players to be frustrated but motivated, believing they can beat the difficult boss that is giving them trouble by simply getting better at the game and therefore being rewarded with the satisfaction of accomplishment. Elden Ring ventures too far into frustration for many of its bosses that it ends up costing the game that satisfation of overcoming difficulties, since many bosses are bested from luck, cheese, coming back when your character is stronger, or a combination of the 3. It doesn't help that you often die in only a few hits, and despite the stakes of Marika, the game still enjoys wasting your time before letting you try again. 
I could talk endlessly about how poorly balanced and unfair and frustrating and bothersome many of the bosses are, but in the face of what the game gets right, this is more of a momentary hiccup that discourages you for a time, until the world pulls you back in with some new enthusiasm. Still, if the game didn't have such a strong world to stand on, then much like BotW, it would never be a 10/10. Except in Elden Ring's case, this is due to things which are horrible, not just ok or good.

items.quote:
**Elden Ring – Arcane Majesty with Flawed Brilliance**  FromSoftware has once again delivered an unforgettable experience with *Elden Ring*, an open-world action RPG that redefines exploration, discovery, and challenge. With a deep yet cryptic narrative, breathtaking landscapes, and unparalleled character customization, the game stands as one of the greatest achievements in gaming history. However, despite its brilliance, *Elden Ring* is not without its flaws—particularly when it comes to enemy balancing and boss design. 
A Cryptic but Captivating Story**  *Elden Ring* follows the tradition of FromSoftware’s storytelling—mysterious, fragmented, and open to interpretation. Rather than spoon-feeding lore, the game immerses players in the **** Lands Between, where the remnants of divine beings struggle for control after the destruction of the titular Elden Ring.  From the enigmatic *Two Fingers* to the tragic demigods, every encounter reveals a piece of the world's history. *Ranni the Witch*, *Radagon*, *Maliketh*—these characters are wrapped in lore so dense that each discovery feels like uncovering a forgotten myth. *Elden Ring* respects the intelligence of its players, rewarding curiosity and persistence with breathtaking revelations.  
Combat – Satisfying, Yet Uneven**  The core of *Elden Ring*’s combat is exceptional, blending precision-based melee with powerful magic and ranged tactics. However, it is far from perfectly balanced.  Some encounters feel exceptionally well-crafted—where skill, patience, and strategy determine victory. Others, however, lean too heavily into unreactable attacks, hyper-aggression, or frustratingly long boss animations where players are forced to watch instead of fight. While this works for cinematic spectacle, it can sometimes lead to moments of frustration, especially in the late game.  Despite this, the sheer variety of approaches makes combat deeply rewarding. Whether wielding colossal greatswords, devastating sorceries, or agile daggers, every playstyle has something unique to offer.  
The Ultimate RPG Playground – Infinite Build Variety**  One of *Elden Ring*’s greatest strengths is its approach to character builds. With countless weapons, spells, and Ashes of War, no two Tarnished are the same.  Want to play as a monstrous berserker wielding a colossal club? A swift and deadly katana master? A spell-slinging sorcerer capable of reshaping reality? The game not only allows this but actively encourages experimentation. *Respec* mechanics make it easy to shift between different playstyles, ensuring that players are never locked into a single approach.  The freedom to mix and match abilities, weapon arts, and armor sets makes *Elden Ring* one of the most versatile RPGs ever made.  
The Lands Between – A World Like No Other**  The world of *Elden Ring* is a masterpiece of environmental storytelling. Unlike many open-world games that rely on quest markers, *Elden Ring* thrives on discovery.  Each biome is distinct, from the golden fields of *Limgrave* to the nightmarish red wastelands of *Caelid*. The eerie underground cities of the *Ainsel River* and *Siofra* add layers of depth, while the frozen peaks of the *Consecrated Snowfield* feel both haunting and beautiful. The verticality of locations like *Leyndell* and *Farum Azula* makes exploration a joy, as every corner hides secrets, treasures, or deadly threats.  Unlike traditional open worlds, *Elden Ring* constantly surprises, offering genuine moments of awe and terror with each new area.  ---## **Recycled Bosses & Overlong Attack Animations**  If *Elden Ring* has one major flaw, it’s the overuse of certain bosses. While fights like *Maliketh* or *Radagon* are spectacular, encountering the same *Tree Sentinel*, *Godskin Duo*, or *Erdtree Avatar* multiple times lessens the impact of these battles.  Additionally, some bosses suffer from excessive animation length, forcing players to spend more time waiting than fighting. Enemies like *Malenia* or *Radagon* often have prolonged, multi-stage attacks that make certain encounters feel unfair rather than challenging. While this is manageable with patience, it sometimes disrupts the otherwise masterful combat flow.  
Verdict: A Flawed Masterpiece**  Despite its imperfections, *Elden Ring* is a landmark in gaming, pushing the boundaries of open-world design and RPG depth. Its cryptic lore, vast build variety, and breathtaking world make it an unforgettable journey. Even with occasional balancing issues and boss design flaws, it remains one of the most rewarding and ambitious RPGs ever created.
